entry.evidence: Accurate dating of the pegmatite is a challenge due to the uncertainty and controversy of crystallization temperature, fractionation model, and cooling mechanism.

sequences.source_document: Published paper PDF (Ore Geology Reviews 153, 105280); XML text used for caption labels only

steps.action: Frame the need to date rare-metal pegmatite mineralization accurately in order to constrain its geodynamic setting.
steps.quote: Accurate determining of the mineralizing age of the deposits is a crucial issue

steps.action: Take from the literature the expected behaviour of each chronometer: zircon metamictization and Pb loss, high closure temperature for cassiterite, and low closure temperature with possible resetting for apatite.
steps.quote: Therefore, it has dating potential, but it may also be reset the age by later thermal events.

steps.action: State the aim: evaluate which minerals from which zones date the pegmatite, find the most suitable dating mineral, and constrain the geodynamic setting.
steps.quote: The focus is to evaluate the applicability of different minerals to dating from different zones in pegmatite

steps.action: Use the group's earlier LA-ICP-MS columbite-(Fe) and zircon dating of zone I (Tang et al., 2017), which gave about 387 Ma, as the prior emplacement age.
steps.quote: revealed that the emplacement age of the Nanping pegmatites occurred

steps.action: Apply the CMS classification (Dill, 2016) to the No. 31 vein and compare it with Cathaysian and Altay pegmatitic rocks in a literature-compiled table.
steps.quote: The No. 31 vein is identified as pegmatite by CMS features.

steps.action: Design the sampling of apatite, cassiterite and CGMs from all five structural zones, and choose weighted means of all concordant data rather than Concordia ages.
steps.quote: we use all Concordance data as the result to obtain the weighted mean age rather than Concordia age

steps.action: Take all zircon data and the zone I CGM data from Tang et al. (2017) and the Cai (2017) thesis from the same institute, without new measurement.
steps.quote: the data of all zircon and CGMs in Zone I are from Tang et al., 2017 and Cai, 2017.

steps.action: Check LA-ICP-MS accuracy against reference materials: QH and Durango apatite, AY-4 cassiterite (153 ± 2.7 Ma returned), and Coltan 139 with 91500 and GJ-1 zircon.
steps.quote: the QH apatite standard (~150 Ma, Chew et al., 2016) was used to verify the analytical accuracy

steps.action: Image the separated apatite grains by BSE to characterize grain size and internal texture.
steps.quote: no bands or other phenomena were found in any samples collected from the five zones in pegmatite.

steps.action: Fit Tera–Wasserburg lower-intercept ages to apatite from the five zones: 216.2, 152.6, 201, 159.1 and 157.5 Ma.
steps.quote: The analytical spots gave a Tera–Wasserburg U–Pb lower intercept age of 152.6 ± 9.8 Ma

steps.action: Image cassiterite by CL and measure its trace elements, separating homogeneous Cass-1 from oscillatory-zoned, chemically distinct Cass-2 of zone II.
steps.quote: Several trace elements show significant differences between cassiterite from zone II and the others

steps.action: Fit Tera–Wasserburg lower-intercept ages to cassiterite: about 350–380 Ma in zones I, III, IV and V, and 149.4 ± 6.4 Ma in zone II.
steps.quote: Cass-1 comes from zones I, III, IV, and V, and their U–Pb ages are 380 ± 20 Ma.

steps.action: Characterize CGM zoning and composition by BSE and EDS (columbite-(Fe) to tantalite-(Mn)) across zones II–V.
steps.quote: show a Ta and Mn increasing trend from zones III, IV, and V to zone II

steps.action: Compute weighted-mean 206Pb/238U CGM ages for zones II–V: 387, 382.3, 383.1 and 370 Ma.
steps.quote: yielding a weighted mean 206Pb/238U age of 382.3 ± 6.7 Ma

steps.action: Compare with the younger zircon ages from zones II and III (Cai, 2017) and attribute them to Pb loss from metamictization in U- and Th-rich zircon.
steps.quote: However, Cai (2017) obtained significantly younger ages

steps.action: Reject the apatite ages of zones I and III as meaningless, because the spots cluster near the upper intercept and do not constrain the lower intercept despite good MSWD.
steps.quote: failing to constrain the lower intercept

steps.action: Pose rivals for the young apatite ages: prolonged slow cooling to the apatite closure temperature, or resetting by a later thermal event.
steps.quote: it is assumed the Nanping pegmatite has a long and slow cooling process

steps.action: Exclude 220 Myr slow cooling: the host rocks were metamorphosed much earlier, the emplacement depth is 4.9 km, and there is no Carboniferous–Jurassic heat source.
steps.quote: we consider that there is no condition for the cooling process of Nanping pegmatite to last 220 Ma.

steps.action: Match the about 150 Ma apatite ages to the Yanshanian orogeny (150–110 Ma) and to published zircon and apatite fission-track ages implying later uplift.
steps.quote: consistent with the dating results of apatite in zones II, IV, and V

steps.action: Keep the interpretation that the vein suffered a severe Yanshanian thermal disturbance at 145–160 Ma.
steps.quote: suffered severe thermal disturbances at 145–160 Ma

steps.action: Compare Cass-1 and Cass-2 crystal morphology and CL activator chemistry with published cassiterite types from different temperatures; conclude both formed at the pegmatitic stage.
steps.quote: are the crystallized in pegmatitic stage

steps.action: Pose rivals for the Cass-2 differences: primary fluid or compositional fluctuation during growth, or transformation by later hydrothermal events.
steps.quote: If the differences caused by later events, suggesting that the later hydrothermal events have transformed the Cass-2.

steps.action: Compare ages across minerals: Cass-1 matches CGMs (370–390 Ma emplacement), and the Cass-2 age matches the reset apatite ages.
steps.quote: The Cass-1 and CGMs have the same age

steps.action: Keep, tentatively, that zone II was most affected by the Yanshanian disturbance, which reset Cass-2; other processes are explicitly not excluded.
steps.quote: we infer that zone II may be most severely affected by thermal disturbance than other zones

steps.action: Check the premise that CGM U–Pb dates are independent of composition: CGMs of different Nb–Ta–Fe–Mn composition give a consistent age; also cite matrix-effect and high-U tests.
steps.quote: the samples of CGMs we analyzed have different major element compositions (Fig. 11), but a consistent age can be obtained.

steps.action: Set the new CGM, cassiterite and zircon ages against the earlier CGM age of 391 ± 4 Ma (Che et al., 2015) and find agreement.
steps.quote: prove the correctness of his conjecture

steps.action: Keep the claim that CGM U–Pb dating gives reliable emplacement and metallogenic ages for pegmatite, from a single magmatic injection.
steps.quote: we propose that CGMs U–Pb dating can provide reliable age constraints in pegmatite.

steps.action: Pose two mechanisms for the larger undercooling of the saccharoidal albite zone: a drop in absolute temperature, or compositional quench by flux enrichment.
steps.quote: There are two mechanisms to change the relative temperature

steps.action: Exclude the temperature-change mechanism, citing no evidence of a low-temperature wall-zone stage and the Cass-2 crystal habit.
steps.quote: it is reasonable to consider the mechanisms 2) are dominate

steps.action: Keep that the micro-fissured saccharoidal albite zone II is more easily altered by later fluids, so its chronological data need caution.
steps.quote: the minerals in this zone would be more affected

steps.action: Use published thermodynamic cooling simulations (London, 2008) to argue that pegmatite crystallization is far shorter than dating precision, so zone sequence cannot be resolved by dating.
steps.quote: the cooling time span of pegmatitic magma would not be long without additional heat supply

tree.answer: Partly: five zones and several minerals act as repeated recorders of the same history
CGM ages consistent across zones and compositions, and agree with Cass-1 and prior CGM ages
CGMs most suitable; emplacement 370–390 Ma; apatite and Cass-2 reset at 145–160 Ma

end.claim: Columbite–tantalite (CGM) U–Pb dating by LA-ICP-MS gives stable, reliable emplacement ages for the Nanping No. 31 rare-metal pegmatite across zones and compositions, unlike apatite, zone II cassiterite and zircon, which can be reset or lose Pb.

decisive_move.sentence: The new weighted-mean CGM U–Pb ages from zones II–V (370–387 Ma) are the evidence for both the emplacement age and the claim that CGMs are the most stable chronometer.

gates.evidence: Action: minerals and zones were chosen to compare chronometers, guided by cited closure-temperature expectations rather than a stated hypothesis (pp. 1-2). Claim: CGM ages could have scattered across zones and compositions, but reliability is judged by agreement with the prior 387 Ma age and with Cass-1, which is partly circular (pp. 11, 13). Registration: the weighted-mean choice is stated, but there is no sign it was fixed before the data were seen; the zone I and III apatite ages were rejected after inspection (pp. 5, 8).

Scanning electron microscopy with BSE and cathodoluminescence detector (Zeiss Gemini Sigma 300 VP) and EDS

the oscillation band in the cassiterite grains might have formed in this period, different from previous studies

limits: The XML text supplied holds only captions, so body steps are located by printed page. No review file was supplied. Sub-claims at different statuses: emplacement age 370–390 Ma is estimate_with_resolution; the 145–160 Ma Yanshanian thermal disturbance is best_explanation (slow cooling excluded; other processes for Cass-2 explicitly 'cannot be excluded', p. 13); greater susceptibility of the saccharoidal albite zone II is best_explanation, weakly supported. The reliability criterion for CGMs is partly circular: agreement with the prior 387 Ma age from the same group's earlier work and with Cass-1. All zircon and zone I CGM data are taken from earlier work (Tang et al., 2017; Cai, 2017), not re-measured. Internal inconsistencies the paper does not address: the AY-4 cassiterite standard returned 153 ± 2.7 Ma against a recommended 158 ± 0.4 Ma, with no comment (p. 5); zone III cassiterite is n = 53 in the text but n = 43 in Fig. 7b; the Fig. 9 and Fig. 11 captions appear swapped; the Fig. 3 caption names 'No.3'; Conclusion 1 says apatite from all zones records the disturbance, while §6.1.1 rejects the zone I and III apatite ages and §6.3 lists zones II, III, V; the data availability statements conflict ('on request' vs 'supplied within the supplementary files'). Inference: the order of analysis and any failed analyses before the reported ones are not documented.

disagreements.target: Cai (2017) zircon U–Pb ages from zones II and III
disagreements.support: The younger zircon ages are attributed to radiation-damage Pb loss, because CGM and Cass-1 ages from the same zones are about 380 Ma.
disagreements.quote: One of the significant reasons for this result is that the zircon formed in the core zone

disagreements.target: Zircon U–Pb as the most widely used pegmatite chronometer (community practice)
disagreements.support: Metamictization, inclusions and Pb loss in pegmatite zircon, shown by the scattered Nanping zircon ages, argue for multi-mineral dating led by CGMs.
disagreements.quote: These features make it challenging to constrain the geochronology of pegmatite by using the zircon U–Pb isotopic system.

disagreements.target: Cassiterite resistance to post-mineralization hydrothermal disturbance (Zhang et al., 2017)
disagreements.support: Zone II Cass-2 gives 149.4 ± 6.4 Ma, coinciding with the reset apatite ages, while other cassiterite gives about 380 Ma.
disagreements.quote: the cassiterite U–Pb system might be reset under severe geological processes

disagreements.target: Successful apatite U–Pb dating of pegmatites (e.g., Dwight et al., 2016)
disagreements.support: Nanping apatite records the 145–160 Ma thermal event or gives unconstrained intercepts, not the emplacement age.
disagreements.quote: the dating results of apatite in pegmatite should be treated with more caution

disagreements.target: Origin of oscillatory zoning in cassiterite (Farmer et al., 1991; Wei et al., 2020)
disagreements.support: Cass-2 zoning coincides with its reset age, suggesting later recrystallization; the authors concede there is no direct evidence linking the two.
disagreements.quote: the oscillation band in the cassiterite grains might have formed in this period, different from previous studies

alternatives_considered.chosen: Weighted mean age of all concordant data
alternatives_considered.reason: Emplacement age already reported; to objectively show the application, limitation, and accuracy of methods in different zones

alternatives_considered.chosen: Common-Pb-unanchored Tera–Wasserburg lower-intercept ages for apatite and cassiterite
alternatives_considered.reason: Low concordance; to reduce common-Pb interference and avoid error from deducting common Pb (Chew et al., 2011)

alternatives_considered.alternatives: 207Pb-based ages; Tera–Wasserburg intercepts from uncorrected data
alternatives_considered.reason: 207Pb and 206Pb are more easily affected by background and common Pb

alternatives_considered.chosen: LA-ICP-MS U–Pb dating of CGMs with Coltan 139
alternatives_considered.reason: LA avoids U-mineral inclusions (vs ID-TIMS); SIMS shows matrix effects tied to Nb/Ta (Legros et al., 2019)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Later thermal resetting of apatite U–Pb at about 150 Ma
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Long, slow cooling of the pegmatite to the apatite closure temperature
alternatives_considered.reason: No heat source, shallow emplacement (4.9 km), host metamorphism much earlier; ages coincide with the Yanshanian orogeny

alternatives_considered.chosen: Cass-2 transformed and reset by a later (Yanshanian) event
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Primary differences from fluid fluctuation or bulk compositional change during growth
alternatives_considered.reason: Cass-2 age coincides with the apatite reset ages; distinct CL and trace elements

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Change of absolute temperature during wall-zone crystallization
alternatives_considered.reason: No evidence of a low-temperature stage; Cass-2 crystal habit shows no temperature change
